sections.title: 1. Core Study Notes
sections.content:
Detailed study guide and resources for Akbar Administration: Land-Revenue System are currently being prepared. Check back soon for comprehensive explanations, summary diagrams, and expert preparation recommendations.

Key Dimensions of Study:

  • Definition, scope, and foundational theories.
  • Relevance to General Studies Paper & Contemporary contexts.
  • Core applications and structural framework.

practiceQuestions.q: Who among the following was the primary architect of Akbar's land-revenue system, known as the Zabti or Dahsala system?
practiceQuestions.sol: Raja Todar Mal, along with Muzaffar Khan Turbati, played the pivotal role in streamlining and structuring Akbar's land-revenue administration, culminating in the Dahsala system. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11, Themes in Indian History - Part II]

practiceQuestions.q: In the context of Akbar's agrarian administration, what was 'Polaj' land?
opts: Land that remained uncultivated for five or more years
Land that was annually cultivated for each crop in succession without being allowed to lie fallow
Land left fallow for one or two years to recover its strength
Barren or rocky wasteland unfit for any agricultural production
practiceQuestions.sol: Polaj was the best quality of land that was cultivated continuously year after year and never allowed to rest fallow. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11, Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q: Which category of land under Akbar's classification was left uncultivated for three to four years?
practiceQuestions.sol: Parauti land was fallow land left uncultivated for a year or two to recover its fertility, whereas Chachar was left uncultivated for three to four years. [Primary Reference: Standard Medieval Indian History, Satish Chandra]

practiceQuestions.q: What does the term 'Dahsala' signify in the land-revenue administration of Akbar?
opts: A tax levied exclusively on cash crops over a ten-month period
A revenue settlement system based on the average prices and yields of the preceding ten years
A system where ten percent of the total revenue was remitted to local chieftains
A military tenure granting ten villages to a mansabdar
practiceQuestions.sol: Introduced in 1580, the Dahsala system calculated the average yield of crops and average prices prevailing over the last ten years (15-24 regnal years) to fix standard revenue rates. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11, Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q: During Akbar's reign, what was the standard unit of land measurement introduced to replace varying local standards?
practiceQuestions.sol: Akbar introduced the standard 'Ilahi Gaz' for linear measurement and the 'Ilahi Bigha' as the standard unit of land area, replacing the Sikandari gaz of the Lodi era. [Primary Reference: Abul Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the primary function of the 'Amil' or 'Amalguzar' in Akbar's administrative machinery?
opts: Assessment and collection of land revenue at the suba/pargana level
Administering criminal justice and maintaining police stations
Auditing imperial palace expenditures and treasury accounts
practiceQuestions.sol: The Amil (or Amalguzar) was the important revenue official responsible for assessing and collecting land revenue in a district or pargana. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: Which measuring instrument made of bamboo strips joined by iron rings was standardized by Akbar to ensure uniform land measurement?
practiceQuestions.sol: Akbar replaced the hemp rope, which used to shrink or expand with moisture, with the bamboo 'tanab' (measuring rod) joined by iron rings, ensuring precise land surveys. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India: From Sultanat to the Mughals]

practiceQuestions.q: What did the term 'Banjar' refer to in the context of Mughal land classification?
opts: Prime agricultural land yielding three harvests a year
Land left uncultivated for five or more years
Grassland reserved exclusively for imperial cavalry horses
Land granted as revenue-free religious endowment (Sayurghal)
practiceQuestions.sol: Banjar was the poorest category of land that remained uncultivated for five or more years and required substantial investment to bring back under cultivation. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11, Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q: In Akbar's revenue administration, what was the primary role of the 'Qanungo'?
opts: Village-level accountant maintaining records of land holdings and revenue payment
Pargana-level hereditary revenue official keeping records of revenue rates, customs, and local land rights
Commander of provincial artillery and gunpowder depots
Imperial spy reporting on corrupt officials directly to the Emperor
practiceQuestions.sol: The Qanungo was a hereditary revenue official at the pargana level who maintained comprehensive records of revenue rates, land revenue history, and local customary rights. [Primary Reference: Irfan Habib, The Agrarian System of Mughal India]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the local village-level accountant and record-keeper called during Akbar's administration?
practiceQuestions.sol: The Patwari was the village accountant who maintained records of land revenue assessed and collected from individual cultivators within the village. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: How did the transition from 'Bataq' (crop-sharing) to 'Zabti' system under Akbar transform the agrarian economy?
opts: It forced peasants to pay revenue exclusively in precious metals, abolishing all barter exchanges.
It shifted assessment from actual physical produce to fixed cash schedules based on standardized measurement and crop yields.
It handed over absolute revenue-collection rights to hereditary zamindars, bypassing state officials.
It exempted cash crops from any taxation to encourage international trade.
practiceQuestions.sol: The Zabti system monetized the rural economy by fixing cash revenue rates (naqdi) per bigha for various crops based on past yields and prices, reducing corruption and state dependence on crop-cutting estimates. [Primary Reference: Irfan Habib, Agrarian System of Mughal India]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the significance of 'Nasaq' (or Kankut) in Mughal land revenue assessment?
opts: It was a rough estimation method based on past inspections or a sample crop-cutting to determine total revenue without detailed bigha-wise measurement.
It was a religious tax levied exclusively on non-Muslim agricultural pilgrims.
It represented the supreme judicial court for land litigation presided over by the Qazi-ul-Quzat.
It was an emergency relief fund distributed among peasants during severe famines.
practiceQuestions.sol: Nasaq (or Kankut) involved rough calculation or guesswork based on past revenue records or inspection of standing crops (sample crop cutting) to assess the revenue demand when full Zabti measurement was impracticable. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: Why did Akbar prefer the cash payment of revenue (Naqdi) over payment in kind (Batail/Galla-bakshi)?
opts: Cash payment eliminated the need for any administrative machinery in rural areas.
Cash facilitated the payment of cash salaries to mansabdars and reduced logistical hurdles of storing and transporting bulky agricultural produce.
Peasants requested cash payments because they had massive surpluses of silver bullion.
Islamic law strictly prohibited any form of crop-sharing taxation.
practiceQuestions.sol: Cash revenue collection was crucial for the Mughal centralized machinery, especially for the Mansabdari system where most nobles were paid cash salaries (or assigned jagirs convertible to cash values), avoiding the storage and spoilage issues of crop shares. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11, Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the role of 'Madad-i-Maash' (or Sayurghal) in the Mughal land administration?
opts: Revenue-free grants of land given to religious scholars, ascetics, and needy persons to secure their loyalty and support scholarship.
Compulsory corvée labor extracted from peasants for building imperial forts and roads.
A heavy tax imposed on newly cleared wastelands to discourage unauthorized land reclamation.
Pensions paid in kind to retired military generals from the imperial treasury.
practiceQuestions.sol: Madad-i-Maash comprised revenue-free land grants issued by the Emperor to pious men, scholars, and religious institutions, which Akbar subjected to careful scrutiny and verification to prevent corruption. [Primary Reference: Abul Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari]

practiceQuestions.q: How did Akbar deal with regional variations in prices while implementing the Dahsala system?
opts: He enforced a single uniform price schedule across the entire Mughal Empire from Bengal to Kabul.
He established localized price schedules (Dastur-ul-amal) for different regions (dasturs) based on local productivity and market prices.
He permitted village headmen to arbitrarily set prices on a daily market basis without state interference.
He relied entirely on the international port prices of Surat and Masulipatnam.
practiceQuestions.sol: To account for regional price differences, the empire was divided into revenue circles (dasturs), and a separate schedule of cash rates (dastur-ul-amal) was drawn up for each crop in each dastur. [Primary Reference: Irfan Habib, Agrarian System of Mughal India]

practiceQuestions.q: Which statement best describes the position of the Zamindars in Akbar's land-revenue architecture?
opts: Zamindars were absolute owners of all land with powers to evict any peasant at will.
Zamindars were autonomous sovereign rulers who paid no allegiance or tax to the Mughal center.
Zamindars held hereditary rights over a share of produce (malikana) or collected revenue on behalf of the state, maintaining armed retainers and acting as intermediaries.
Zamindars were salaried imperial civil servants appointed annually by the Diwan.
practiceQuestions.sol: Zamindars were not government officials in the strict sense, but hereditary intermediaries who held superior rights over land (malikana) and assisted in revenue collection while maintaining independent military retinues. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11, Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the administrative purpose behind Akbar's classification of land into Polaj, Parauti, Chachar, and Banjar?
opts: To levy differential tax rates that incentivized the cultivation of fallow and wasteland while discouraging over-cultivation of prime land.
To distribute land strictly based on the caste hierarchy of rural communities.
To determine which lands should be permanently flooded for irrigation reservoirs.
To allocate hunting grounds exclusively for the Mughal imperial court.
practiceQuestions.sol: Land classification was designed to ensure equitable taxation and incentivize agricultural expansion. Fallow lands (Parauti, Chachar) were assessed at lower rates when brought back under cultivation, and Banjar was given concessions to encourage reclamation. [Primary Reference: Irfan Habib, Agrarian System of Mughal India]

practiceQuestions.q: How did Akbar's revenue administration protect peasants against unexpected crop failures or natural calamities?
opts: By granting permanent tax exemption to all farmers across the empire regardless of harvest.
Through remissions of revenue (takhfif) proportional to crop damage and advancing agricultural loans (taccavi or sondhar) for seeds and cattle.
By confiscating private moneylenders' assets and distributing them among famine victims.
By forcing peasants to migrate immediately to urban manufacturing centers.
practiceQuestions.sol: The state maintained a humane approach during crises by granting revenue remissions when crops failed and providing low-interest agricultural loans known as 'taccavi' (or sondhar) to help peasants procure seeds and implements. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11, Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the institutional relationship between the 'Diwan' at the provincial level and the provincial governor ('Subadar') under Akbar?
opts: The Diwan was completely subordinate to the Subadar and acted as his personal secretary.
The Diwan was independent of the Subadar, reporting directly to the imperial Diwan-i-Kul, thereby establishing a system of checks and balances in provincial administration.
The Subadar handled all financial matters while the Diwan commanded the military forces.
Both offices were combined into a single post held by the same military commander.
practiceQuestions.sol: To prevent abuse of power, Akbar organized provincial administration on the principle of checks and balances. The provincial Diwan was in charge of revenue and finance, independent of the Subadar (governor), and reported directly to the imperial center. [Primary Reference: Abul Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari]

practiceQuestions.q: Why is Akbar's land revenue reform considered a major milestone in Indian agrarian history?
opts: It completely abolished the private ownership of land across the subcontinent forever.
It substituted arbitrary exactions with a rationalized, systematic survey-based assessment, ensuring predictable state revenue and protecting cultivators from capricious local lords.
It introduced mechanized steam tractors and chemical fertilizers into Indian farming.
It made agriculture completely tax-free for all strata of society.
practiceQuestions.sol: Akbar's reforms replaced chaotic, arbitrary revenue demands with scientific land surveys, standardized measurement units, dependable yield averages, and cash schedules, forming the bedrock of Mughal fiscal stability and administrative efficiency. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11, Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Akbar's Land-Revenue System:
1. The Dahsala system was introduced by Akbar in the 24th year of his reign (1580 AD) under the guidance of Raja Todar Mal.
2. Under the Zabti system, the state revenue demand was fixed in cash based on the average yield and average prices of the preceding ten years.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are accurate. In 1580 (24th regnal year), Akbar instituted the Dahsala system where average produce and prices of the past 10 years (15th to 24th regnal years) were calculated to formulate permanent revenue rates under the Zabti framework. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11, Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements about land categories under Akbar's administration:
1. 'Polaj' land was cultivated continuously every year without leaving it fallow.
2. 'Chachar' land was left fallow for three to four years to recover its lost fertility.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Akbar's administration categorized agricultural land based on its fertility and cultivation cycle: Polaj (cultivated annually), Parauti (fallow for 1-2 years), Chachar (fallow for 3-4 years), and Banjar (uncultivated for 5+ years). [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding measurement units and officials in Akbar's revenue administration:
1. The 'Ilahi Gaz' replaced the Sikandari Gaz as the standard unit of linear measurement.
2. The 'Amil' was a village-level accountant responsible for maintaining records of land holdings.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: Akbar introduced the Ilahi Gaz (substituting Sikandari Gaz). Statement 2 is incorrect: The Patwari was the village-level accountant, whereas the Amil (or Amalguzar) was a district/pargana-level revenue assessment and collection officer. [Primary Reference: Abul Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements about revenue collection methods under Akbar:
1. 'Batail' or crop-sharing was completely outlawed and banned across the entire empire upon the introduction of the Zabti system.
2. 'Kankut' or Nasaq involved estimating the crop yield by inspecting standing crops or relying on past revenue records without strict bigha-by-bigha measurement.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is incorrect because crop-sharing (Batail) was not completely banned; it continued to be used in areas where Zabti measurement was impractical or during crop failures. Statement 2 is correct regarding Kankut/Nasaq. [Primary Reference: Irfan Habib, Agrarian System of Mughal India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the revenue officials in Akbar's administration:
1. The 'Qanungo' was a pargana-level hereditary official who maintained records of local land revenue rules, customs, and crop rates.
2. The 'Karuri' was an official appointed by Akbar to collect one krore (ten million) dams of revenue and survey unmeasured lands.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Qanungos were vital pargana record-keepers. In 1574-75, Akbar appointed Kararis across the empire to measure lands and collect revenue targeted at one crore dams per jurisdiction. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the welfare and relief measures in Akbar's agrarian system:
1. 'Taccavi' loans were advanced by the state to cultivators to help them purchase agricultural seeds, cattle, and implements during times of distress.
2. State revenue demands were rigid and inflexible, never granting any remissions even during severe droughts or famines.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: Taccavi (or sondhar) loans were extended for agricultural rehabilitation. Statement 2 is incorrect because the Mughal administration routinely granted revenue remissions (takhfif) when crops failed due to natural calamities. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11, Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Zamindars in the Mughal agrarian structure:
1. Zamindars were created solely by Akbar and did not exist in India prior to the Mughal Empire.
2. Zamindars held hereditary rights over a share of produce (malikana) and often maintained independent fortresses and armed retainers.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is incorrect because zamindars existed in India long before the Mughals (such as autonomous chieftains and intermediate revenue collectors). Statement 2 is correct: they held malikana rights and maintained military retinues. [Primary Reference: Irfan Habib, Agrarian System of Mughal India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Tanab and Survey instruments under Akbar:
1. Akbar replaced the hemp rope measurement with a bamboo rod ('tanab') joined by iron rings to prevent inaccuracies caused by weather changes.
2. The 'Ilahi Bigha' was standardized as the official unit of land area across the empire.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Hemp ropes shrank in winter and expanded in rains, so Akbar substituted them with iron-ringed bamboo tanabs. The Ilahi Bigha was established as the standard land area unit. [Primary Reference: Abul Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding provincial financial checks and balances in Akbar's administration:
1. The provincial Diwan was placed directly under the command of the provincial Subadar to ensure unity of command.
2. The imperial news-writers (Waqia-navis) and spies reported directly to the Emperor, providing oversight on both provincial governors and revenue officials.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is incorrect because the provincial Diwan was independent of the Subadar to check corruption. Statement 2 is correct: Waqia-navis and imperial intelligence agents reported directly to the Emperor to maintain administrative accountability. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding 'Madad-i-Maash' grants under Akbar:
1. Madad-i-Maash were revenue-free land grants given to religious scholars, holy men, and the destitute.
2. Akbar completely abolished the verification and renewal of these grants, allowing holders to enjoy hereditary tax exemptions without any state interference forever.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: Madad-i-Maash were sustenance grants for pious and needy persons. Statement 2 is incorrect because Akbar exercised strict personal scrutiny over these grants, reduced fraudulent claims, and required periodic imperial confirmation, rather than giving unchecked hereditary rights. [Primary Reference: Abul Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari]
